newsitem.title: USA: Bonds, stocks rally, but Dow loses steam.
newsitem.headline: Bonds, stocks rally, but Dow loses steam.

text.p: Stocks and bonds rallied on positive economic news on Thursday, but blue-chip shares lost steam to end only slightly higher as profit-takers squelched a rally for the second day in a row.
The dollar surged against the Japanese yen amid worries a worsening Southeast Asian currency crisis could damage Japan's fragile economy.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 13.71 points at 7,942.03. The blue-chip index has soared nearly 880 points this summer on the back of moderate economic growth and subdued inflation.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,516 to 1,258 on heavy volume of 530 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index gained 3.29 points to 1,586.69.
Stocks gained some support from the bond market, which rallied after the government reported the consumer price index rose a mere 0.2 percent in July, in line with forecasts.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose nearly a full point, lowering its yield to 6.55 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.63 percent. Bond prices and yield's move in opposite directions.

Despite the retreat in bond interest rates from a recent peak of 6.70 percent, the stock market still felt the long-bond yield was still high. The rate is one-quarter point higher than the 6.33 percent rate on July 30, when the Dow stood at a then-record 8,254.89.
Analysts said investors clearly remained edgy, selling stocks into any market strength as rates remained higher than a week ago.

"There were great expectations built into the (stock) market then," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "Just last week, people were talking about interest rates going to 6 percent."
Stocks mirrored Wednesday's pattern, as the market burst higher at the open in relief over the tame inflation data, only to sharply reverse course later in the session.

In currency markets, the yen slumped across the board after Indonesia announced a de facto float of its currency Thursday following similar actions by neighboring countries in recent weeks. Its currency, the rupiah, fell about 5 percent overnight, hitting a record low.
Traders feared Japan might be forced to devalue its own currency to compete with other Pacific Rim countries.
In New York trading, the dollar topped 118 yen for the first time since falling more than 4 percent last week. It ended at 117.85 yen, up from 115.65 at Wednesday's close.
The dollar also rose against the mark, but its gains were limited by the advance of the German currency against the yen. The dollar ended at 1.8395 marks, up from 1.8345 Wednesday.

Orange juice prices fell sharply after a consulting firm predicted a much larger than expected orange crop this year in Florida. At the New York Cotton Exchange, frozen concentrated orange juice for September delivery dropped 9.60 cents a pound to close at 69.65 cents, its lowest level since February 1993.
In other markets, soybean prices fell on forecasts for rain later this week in dry areas of the Midwest and most oil prices closed lower on profit-taking after this week's rally in gasoline.
Overseas, the London Stock Exchange's FTSE 100 fell 12.3 points, or 0.25 percent to 4,991.3. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average rose 214.02 points, or 1.13 percent, to 19,222.62.
